title: Seek by desiring (Anselm, Proslogion 1)
hookLine: let me seek thee in longing, let me long for thee in seeking
tomorrow: what color is a soul that's coming back to life?

cards: Scrolling listings for a house you can't afford. Rewatching the trailer for a trip you haven't booked. Wanting can be its own kind of looking.
Anselm, a monk who became archbishop of Canterbury, opens a short book, the Proslogion, by turning that into prayer. But a few pages later, the same man builds an argument.
So where does the search for God start: in the heart, or in the head?

teach.b: First, the room. Anselm starts by talking to himself: put down the work, step away from the tugging thoughts, go into the inner room of your mind, shut out everything but God, and shut the door.
He admits he has never seen God's face and doesn't know where to look. He was made to see God, he says, and hasn't yet done what he was made for. Third, the line.
He can't seek unless God teaches him, or find unless God shows himself.

teach.h: SEEK IN LONGING, LONG IN SEEKING.
teach.b: So he asks: let me seek thee in longing, let me long for thee in seeking; let me find thee in love, and love thee in finding.
The chapter ends: he doesn't seek to understand so that he can believe; he believes so that he can understand. Fourth, the debate.

In the very next chapter Anselm offers a well-known argument for God. Later, Thomas Aquinas, also a saint, answered that this argument doesn't prove God to us, and reasoned instead from the world we can see.
One: the search starts in longing and faith, and reasoning grows inside it. The other: reasoning from creation can walk a seeker toward the door before the longing comes. The Church honors both men.

how: Catholics honor both Anselm and Thomas Aquinas as saints and Doctors of the Church; Anselm's phrase 'faith seeking understanding' is often used to describe Catholic theology.

o: a vow to want nothing at all in this life
proving God exists with one strong argument
searching for God by longing for him

games.q: seek by desiring — tap the pairs.
p: reasoned from the world we can see

s: Anselm was a cold logician who began with pure argument
his book opens as a prayer admitting he has never seen God's face.
Anselm says he believes so that he can understand
the search starts inside faith, not before it.
Aquinas agreed that Anselm's argument proves God to anyone
he said it doesn't prove God to us, and reasoned from the world we see.

games.q: Mia says, "nobody can argue me into God." you're asked to give the best case for the Aquinas side. what is it?
o: reasoning from the world can walk a seeker toward the door.
a strong enough argument will force anyone to believe.
if the logic is airtight, faith doesn't really matter.
games.why: Aquinas reasoned from the world we can see, as a road toward God, not a trap. Anselm began in longing prayer. the Church honors both.

practice: Close your eyes and shut a door, a real one or one in your mind. Say Anselm's line slowly, half on each breath: let me seek thee in longing; let me long for thee in seeking.
If the words aren't yours, stay with the longing itself, and let the wanting and the looking take turns.

wordCard.voice: Seek by desiring. Anselm's circle: the longing sends him searching, and the searching makes him long.

orig.note: Latin for by desiring: Anselm asks to seek God by desiring, and to desire by seeking.

carryVoice: Your line: seek and long. In Anselm's prayer, each one keeps the other going. Goodnight for now.

sources.ref: Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 2, a. 1, reply to obj. 2; a. 3
